characterList.description: A CNN news anchor. White male with short brown hair, wearing a dark suit, blue shirt and blue tie.
characterList.name: Jonathan Mann

characterList.description: A man speaking in a thick accent while measuring radiation levels. Visible only from the neck up.
characterList.name: Expert 1 (unidentified)

characterList.description: A man in white protective gear holding a yellow radiation detector.
characterList.name: Expert 2 (unidentified)

characterList.description: Two men in white protective gear collecting samples in a snowy forest.
characterList.name: Greenpeace activists

characterList.description: Director General of the IAEA. Asian male with short black hair, wearing a dark suit, white shirt and a red tie with white stripes.
characterList.name: Yukiya Amano

content_metadata.description: This video segment from CNN focuses on the crisis following a nuclear catastrophe in Japan, exploring the escalation of the incident, international responses, and the role of the IAEA. It includes reporting, expert opinions, and detailed analysis, highlighting concerns about radiation levels, transparency issues, and discussions on nuclear safety.

qAndA.answer: The device is red and black.
qAndA.question: What is the color of the radiation measuring device held by Expert 1 in the beginning of the video?

qAndA.answer: The expert states that people living outside the evacuation zone could exceed the maximum annual permitted radiation dose in just a few days, highlighting a serious health risk.
qAndA.question: Based on the Greenpeace expert's statement, what specific concern is raised regarding the radiation levels outside the evacuation zone?

qAndA.answer: Amano acknowledges initial difficulties in receiving information.
qAndA.question: What was the issue regarding information transparency at the start of the crisis according to Yukiya Amano?

qAndA.answer: He references a 2007 earthquake at another Tepco plant, which revealed that the reactor had been built on a fault line despite the IAEA's prior assessments.
qAndA.question: What past event does Jonathan Mann use to challenge the IAEA's effectiveness in preventing nuclear disasters?

qAndA.answer: While acknowledging the severity of the situation, he emphasizes the importance of international cooperation and expresses cautious optimism for overcoming the crisis. This suggests a mood of determination and resilience.
qAndA.question: What mood does Yukiya Amano convey through his concluding statement?

activities.description: Interview with Yukiya Amano about the nuclear crisis in Japan.

characterInteraction.description: Jonathan Mann directly questions Yukiya Amano about the crisis, the IAEA's response, and potential areas for improvement.

narrativeProgression.description: The interview begins with Jonathan Mann questioning the reliability of information and the progress of the situation's management.
Discussion centers on transparency, the role of the IAEA in coordinating international assistance, and the continued challenges faced by Japan.
Jonathan Mann challenges the IAEA's role in preventing the crisis, highlighting past concerns and urging a more proactive international response.

climax.description: The climax in the storyline of 'The Escalating Nuclear Crisis in Japan' occurs when Greenpeace reveals high radiation levels outside the evacuation zone. In 'International Response & the Role of the IAEA,' it is when Jonathan Mann challenges the IAEA's past effectiveness and calls for a stronger response.

storylines.description: The video comprises two main storylines: The escalating nuclear crisis in Japan and the international response to it. It showcases independent radiation findings, expert perspectives, and examines the role of international bodies in crisis management.

content_metadata.title: Crisis in Japan - Analyzing the Nuclear Emergency

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: The UN's chief nuclear inspector watches a crisis unfold in his own homeland.
Does he even know what to do about it and is it time for him to do something?
Also, I have over 1,300 counts per second.
Well, normally 30.
So it's a...
It's a thick, sufficiently higher here.
Waying the risks and issuing a warning, environmental activists carry out their own tests outside Japan's
cripple nuclear evacuation zone, all that and more here at the International Desk.
Back to our top story.
Now Fukushima's nuclear power plant, a catastrophe Japan can't seem to control.
And test show, new reasons to worry.
Radiation in pooled water in the building housing reactor number two, 10 million times higher than normal.
Levels of radioactive iodine and seawater offshore more than 1,800 times higher than normal.
Numbers shown nearly 60% of Japanese don't approve of the government's handling of the crisis.
It's rapidly becoming a global problem, though.
Trace amounts of radiation from Fukushima have been detected as far away as Sweden and the US.
The US has already taken steps to protect its citizens in Japan, giving them potassium iodide pills.
Meantime, Greenpeace is conducting its own study of radiation just outside the evacuation zone.
We talked with the group's nuclear expert about what they found.
We are measuring reactivity at today at the EUP village and we're measuring very high levels of reactivity.
So people living there and there's still people living there, they would exceed the maximum annual permitted dose in just a couple of days.
And there's still thousands of people living there.
And they are clearly at risk.
Clearly at risk, joining us now from Vienna, Austria, Yuki Amano, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency.
Thanks so much for talking with us, sir.
It seems like there is surprising and terrifying news just about every day.
Today we're learning about radiation levels in the seawater, 1800 times higher than normal.
Water levels inside the turbine building, reactor number two containing radioactive iodine levels,
10 million times higher than normal.
So let me ask you, as this unfolds, are you confident that this problem is being solved?
That Teppo, which is operating the plants, is being honest and transparent?
Does the IAEA even have all the facts and know what's going on?
Jonathan, I am following the situation every day.
And this is a very serious accident by any standard.
Therefore, the most important thing for now is to overcome this crisis situation.
The IAEA is doing everything in its power.
You say the IAEA is doing everything in its power.
Is it getting enough information to do everything in its power?
I ask you that question because the earthquake and tsunami struck on March 11th.
Most of us didn't find out around the world about the problem at this plant until March 12th.
When we literally saw on television the explosion published accounts,
and I think the IAEA will confirm that your agency didn't get all the information it wanted.
It was still waiting for information on March 16th.
So once again, let me ask you, is Teppo and are the Japanese government officials
you're talking to telling you everything you need to know as quickly as you need to know it?
At the beginning, we had some difficulties.
But I went to Tokyo and I talked to Prime Minister Khan
and asked to facilitate the flow of information.
Prime Minister Khan promised me the highest level of transparency
and later the flow of information improved.
So are you endorsing now what is happening now that the management Teppo
and the Japanese government are bringing to the task?
Is the IAEA fully confident that the work being done there
is exactly what outside experts would approve of?
It is difficult to say what is right and what is wrong.
As I said, the accident is not yet over.
And the most important thing is to overcome this difficulty.
After the situation is stabilized, we will send expert missions
and we will learn lessons.
But for now, let's concentrate to overcome this crisis.
Let me ask you about the opportunity that the IAEA and Teppo had to prevent this crisis.
Back in 2007, as you well know, there was an earthquake at another Teppo plant.
It was twice as strong as that reactor had been built to withstand.
And it turned out that Teppo didn't know until then that the reactor it had built
was actually on a fault.
The IAEA has known about earthquake problems in Japan.
It has told outside officials about it.
But how hard did your agency press Japanese authorities
before this disaster after the last one when the problems were obvious even to you?
The IAEA established safety standard
and IAEA sent missions to provide advice to Japan and other countries.
The responsibility lies on each state.
But thinking retrospectively, the measures that were taken were no sufficient.
Therefore, when the situation is stabilized,
we need to send missions to assess the accident
and review the situation and we need to learn lessons.
Well, one would suggest that maybe you need to do more.
The sense that many outside experts have is that Japan is no longer capable
of solving this problem on its own.
So let me ask you as Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency,
if it's time for someone outside of Japan to impress on the Japanese government
that this needs to be a global effort to solve the problem,
whether the IAEA should do that, make that demand,
and whether the IAEA and you should take over now.
It is very important that the international community help Japan.
The IAEA is mandated to coordinate the assistance
from international organizations and other countries.
We have many offers from various countries and we channel it to Japan.
IAEA itself sent missions to monitor the radio activity.
We sent missions to monitor food staff and we have
from position people to coordinate the activities in assistance in Japan.
We will continue to do our utmost to help Japan.
International community need to stand by Japan.
Stand by Japan, Yuki Amano, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency.
Thanks so much for this.
